chapter.title: Kicking from the hips

cards.body: Kicking harder can move you slower, and the shallow end proves it every evening. Back to the bed: the water is already holding you up, so **your kick's first job is to keep your legs lying flat on it**, not to shove you across. A small, steady flutter does that. A big thrash pulls the sheets off.
cards.simpler: Kicking harder can actually make you slower, and you can see it at any shallow end in the evening. Think of the water like a bed you are lying on. It already holds you up. So **your kick's first job is to keep your legs lying flat on the water**, not to push you across the pool. A small, steady flutter does that. A big, wild kick is like thrashing in bed and pulling the sheets off.

cards.prompt: Sam and Jo race across the shallow end on kickboards. Sam kicks huge, knees pumping like riding a bike, spray up to the ceiling lights. Jo kicks small, legs long, feet flopping. Who gets there first?

options.text: Sam. All that splash is power.
Jo, with the small, floppy kick.
A tie. The kick barely matters.

whyNot.a: That's effort, not speed: Sam's bent knees push the shins forward into the water, braking every kick.
whyNot.c: That's mixing up 'the kick isn't the main engine' with 'the kick doesn't matter': a good kick keeps you level and moves you, a bad one sinks and slows you.

cards.reteach: Water pushes back on anything moving forward through it. Big bent-knee kicks shove your shins forward into the water, so much of every kick fights you. A small kick from long legs pushes water behind you and keeps you flat on the bed.

cards.title: Where the kick comes from
cards.body:
**The kick starts at your hips**, not your knees. Think of each leg as one long noodle hanging from your hip: the thigh moves first, and the knee just softens a little on the way down.

Your ankles stay loose, like socks on a washing line. When they flop, the top of each foot bends back and pushes water behind you, the way a flipper does.

Keep it small. Your feet only part about a shoebox length, roughly 30 cm, with your heels just breaking the surface.
cards.simpler: **The kick starts at your hips**, not your knees. Picture each leg as a long noodle hanging from your hip. The thigh moves first, and the knee bends a little on the way down. Keep your ankles loose, like socks on a washing line. When they flop, the top of your foot pushes water behind you, like a flipper. Keep it small. Your feet open about a shoebox apart, roughly 30 cm, with your heels just breaking the surface.

cards.title: Priya's 12 metres
cards.body: Priya, 34, holds a kickboard at the shallow end and kicks like she's late for a train. Knees up, spray everywhere, a toddler in the next lane cheering her on. Twenty seconds later she has moved about 3 metres and her legs are sinking. She tries again with long legs, floppy feet and a kick half the size. She crosses the 12-metre width in about 30 seconds and can still chat at the end.
cards.simpler: Priya, 34, holds a kickboard at the shallow end and kicks like she's late for a train. Her knees come up, water sprays everywhere, and a toddler in the next lane cheers. After 20 seconds she has moved about 3 metres, and her legs are sinking. Then she tries again with **long legs, floppy feet and a kick half the size**. She crosses the 12-metre width in about 30 seconds and can still chat at the end.

cards.prompt: You're holding the wall, face in, kicking. Your legs feel heavy and you're churning up foam. Which cue do you give yourself?

options.text: Bend your knees more for a bigger push.
Long legs from the hips, loose ankles, smaller kick.
Pull your toes up toward your shins for a stronger paddle.

whyNot.a: That's a cycling kick, not a flutter kick: bent knees drive your shins forward and brake you.
whyNot.c: That's a standing foot, not a flipper: toes pulled up turn your foot into a brake, so you stay put.

cards.reteach: Think about where the water goes. A long leg with a floppy foot sends water behind you, so you move forward. Bent knees or stiff, hooked feet catch the water like a brake, so you work hard and stay put.

cards.title: Why bigger is slower
cards.body:
You'd think a bigger kick means more push. Often it's the opposite: **a kick that goes deep or bends the knee hard creates a lot of drag**, which eats up much of the push it makes. Your legs stop being a tail and start acting like an anchor.

Terry Laughlin, who created the Total Immersion method, taught that a long, balanced body matters more than strong legs. The kick keeps you level. Being long does the travelling.

Same with your head. Lift it high to look for the wall and your hips sink, like sitting up in bed. Lift it to breathe, then face back down.
cards.simpler: A bigger kick seems like more push, but **a kick that goes deep or bends the knee hard creates a lot of drag** and wastes much of its own push. Your legs start acting like an anchor. Terry Laughlin, creator of the Total Immersion method, taught that a long, balanced body matters more than strong legs. The kick keeps you level. Being long carries you forward. Lift your head high and your hips sink. Lift it to breathe, then look down.

cards.body: A man in a red cap kicks on his board for a full minute and has barely moved, puffing hard, sure he's just bad at this. His feet are hooked up as if he's waiting at a bus stop, so every kick catches the water like a brake. How to spot it: if you're working hard and the wall isn't getting closer, check your ankles and let them flop.
cards.simpler: A man in a red cap kicks on his board for a full minute and has hardly moved. He is out of breath and sure he's just bad at this. His feet are bent up, as if he's waiting at a bus stop, so **every kick catches the water like a brake**. Here's how to spot it: if you're working hard and the wall isn't getting closer, check your ankles and let them flop.

cards.prompt: Halfway across with your kickboard, your legs are sinking and you're out of breath. What's the most likely fix?

options.text: Kick bigger and harder to lift your legs back up.
Lift your head to see how far the wall is.
Make the kick smaller and steadier from the hips, ankles floppy.

whyNot.a: That's the thrash, not the flutter: a bigger kick bends the knees, drags more and tires you faster.
whyNot.b: That's sitting up in bed, not lying on it: a high head drops your hips and sinks your legs further.

cards.reteach: Sinking legs and a racing heart usually mean the kick has grown too big. Shrink it back to a quick, small flutter from the hips, feet loose, heels just breaking the surface. Your legs come back up because you're lying flat again, not because you pushed harder.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Kick from your hips with long legs and floppy ankles, small and steady, about a shoebox apart. **Big bent-knee kicks feel strong but brake you**, and keeping your legs flat on the water matters more than power.
cards.simpler: Kick from your hips with long legs and floppy ankles. Keep it small and steady, with your feet about a shoebox apart. **Big bent-knee kicks feel strong but work like a brake**. Keeping your legs flat on the water matters more than power.

cards.body:
Tonight, lie face down across the end of your bed so your legs hang off from mid-thigh, then flutter small kicks from your hips with floppy ankles for 20 seconds. If your heels swing up past your knees, you're bending too much.

Tomorrow: the arms, and why your swimming breath works backwards.
cards.simpler: Tonight, lie face down across the end of your bed so your legs hang off from about the middle of your thighs. For 20 seconds, **flutter small kicks from your hips**, keeping your ankles floppy. If your heels swing up past your knees, that's a sign you're bending too much. Keep your legs long and let your hips do the work. Tomorrow we look at the arms, and at why breathing while you swim works backwards.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now kick across the width of the pool on a kickboard with a small, loose kick from the hips, face in and breathing out.

dubious_claims: Bed drill: 'If your knees keep thumping the mattress, they're bending too much.' A straight-legged kick from the hips is what drives the knees into the mattress. Bending the knee lifts the foot instead.
'a kick that goes deep or bends the knee hard drags you back about as much as it drives you on': overstated, and no source is given for it.
Mistake card: a beginner kicking hard for a full minute 'ends up exactly where he started' is an exaggeration.
Ex1 feedback c ('That's underselling the legs') doesn't name a specific confusion the way the other feedback lines do.
repairedFrom.why: The bed drill can't work: lying flat on a mattress, a straight-legged kick from the hips is exactly what thumps the knees and thighs down, so the test flags the right kick as wrong, and the card ends the chapter after the 'tomorrow' teaser.
repairedFrom.fix: Rewrite the drill: 'Lie face down with your hips at the foot of the bed and your legs hanging off from mid-thigh, then flutter 20 seconds; if your heels swing past your knees, you're bending too much.' Then move the 'Tomorrow: the arms...' line so it comes after this card.
